This legal position underscores why AI should not be positioned as an autonomous decision-maker but rather as a supportive adjunct.
At an institutional level, governance should incorporate continuous algorithmic monitoring, clear delineation of responsibility, and processes for appeal and oversight.

Clinicians must understand the strengths and limitations of model architectures, data representativeness, and bias sources to critically interpret outputs rather than accepting them as objective truths.
Trainees must, therefore, be formally instructed to analyze AI-assisted outputs within pathology practice.

Programs should incorporate workflows without the use of AI to ensure learners maintain independent clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy and metacognitive awareness, preserving the human expertise at the heart of clinical decision-making.

Learners and clinicians should be able to articulate how AI tools have influenced their reasoning, justify their reliance on specific outputs, and clearly communicate uncertainty to colleagues and patients.

unlisted_practices: Embed AI literacy, diagnostic skepticism, and ethical transparency within competency-based post-graduate curricula and accreditation milestones.
Train learners to blind-review cases, then consult AI outputs, and perform structured reflective decision audits on whether AI changed their diagnosis.
Use discrepancies among AI models as teaching opportunities by having trainees compare and justify conflicting outputs against guidelines.
Use simulation-based practice and confidence-calibration exercises to train clinicians in working with AI.
Adopt a decision-making matrix defining which pathology tasks may be delegated to AI, delegated with caution, or never delegated, with bias mitigations.
Conduct periodic bias audits and require disaggregated performance data to monitor AI equity across demographics.
